unit.title: Electrical Circuits
unit.blurb: Current and voltage, circuit symbols, series and parallel circuits, combining cells in batteries, and calculating resistance with Ohm's law.

O1.t: Describe current and voltage, how they are measured, and use standard circuit symbols.

O2.t: Describe current and voltage in series circuits and how to connect ammeters and voltmeters.

O3.t: Describe current and voltage in parallel circuits and the limits of circuit models.

O4.t: Explain the effect of connecting cells in series and in parallel.

O5.t: Calculate resistance using resistance = voltage ÷ current.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 12: Electrical Circuits.

Every electrical device has a circuit: a path for current, from a power source, through wires and components, and back again. Understanding circuits helps us stay safe at home and design devices that waste less energy.

An electric current is a flow of electric charge: moving electrons. Think of it like water flowing through a pipe. Current is measured in amperes with an ammeter, and it only flows around a complete, closed circuit.
Voltage, or potential difference, is the push that drives the charge, like water pressure. Cells, batteries and generators provide it. Voltage is measured in volts with a voltmeter.
Circuit diagrams use standard symbols that engineers everywhere understand: cells, lamps, switches, resistors, ammeters, voltmeters, buzzers and more. A switch opens or closes the circuit.

captions: In a series circuit, components are connected end to end in a single loop, like a one-lane road. The current is the same at every point, but the voltage from the cell is shared between the components. With two identical lamps, each gets half.

Add a third lamp and the voltage is shared even more, so all the lamps get dimmer. And if one lamp breaks, the only path is broken, so every lamp goes out, just like traffic stopping on a closed one-lane road.
To measure current, connect an ammeter in series, so the current flows through it. To measure voltage, connect a voltmeter in parallel, across the component.

captions: In a parallel circuit, components sit on separate branches, like lanes on a highway. Each branch gets the full voltage, so adding identical lamps doesn't make them dimmer. If one lamp fails, the others stay on, which is why homes are wired in parallel.

The total current is the sum of the branch currents: three 1-amp lamps draw 3 amps. Road analogies help us picture circuits, but every model has limitations. As scientific understanding grows, scientists develop better models and analogies.

captions: A cell stores energy in chemicals. In a closed circuit, they react and the energy is transferred by electricity. A battery is two or more cells joined. In the symbol, the longer line is the positive terminal.
Connect cells in series, positive to negative, and their voltages add up: four 3-volt cells give 12 volts. The current capacity stays the same.

Connect cells in parallel, and the voltage stays the same as one cell, but the capacity increases, so the battery lasts longer. Rechargeable batteries cost more at first, but are cheaper and greener over time.

captions: Resistance is how much a component opposes the current, measured in ohms. By Ohm's Law, more voltage gives more current, and more resistance gives less. Resistance equals voltage divided by current.
Example: a light bulb runs on 230 volts with a current of 0.5 amps. Resistance equals 230 divided by 0.5, which is 460 ohms. Electric heaters use resistance to turn electrical energy into heat.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What instrument measures current, and how is it connected? Pause the video now.
Answer: An ammeter, connected in series.
Question 2: What happens to the other lamps if one breaks in a series circuit? Pause the video now.
Answer: They all go out.
Question 3: Four 3-volt cells are connected in series. What is the total voltage? Pause the video now.
Answer: 12 volts.
Question 4: Calculate the resistance: 12 volts and 2 amps. Pause the video now.
Answer: 6 ohms.
